title: Platform systems & services: dashboards, runbooks, how-tos, retrospectives and roadmap
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical platform engineering playbook for Redwood's hosted, dedicated, and private inference offerings. It aggregates runbooks, dashboard and alerting standards, common how-tos, a lightweight retrospective summary of major initiatives in the last two quarters, and a quarter-level roadmap for visibility across the team. The goal is to provide a single reference engineers and on-call responders can use for triage, runbook execution, and planning.

Contents
1. Purpose and scope
2. Ownership and contacts
3. Platform systems and service inventory
4. Dashboards and alerting standards
5. Key runbooks (high-priority incidents)
6. How-tos (dashboards, alerts, and runbook updates)
7. Retrospective: Q3-Q4 2026 initiatives and action items
8. Roadmap: Q1-Q2 2027 highlights
9. Appendix: SLO table, escalation matrix, and example queries

1) Purpose and scope
This document covers the production-facing platform stack that supports Redwood's hosted, dedicated, and private inference offerings. It is intended for: on-call engineers, platform service owners, SREs, and engineering managers who operate or modify platform systems. Topics included: monitoring, alerting, runbooks, ownership, and short-term roadmap items that affect availability and developer productivity.

4) Dashboards and alerting standards
Intro: Dashboards and alerts are the primary signal paths for platform reliability. Follow these standards when creating or modifying dashboards/alerts.

Dashboard standards
- Ownership: every dashboard must have an explicit owner and written purpose statement in the dashboard description.
- Naming convention: platform/<service>/<purpose> e.g., platform/api-gateway/latency-and-errors.
- Template: each service dashboard must include the following sections: Overview (latency, error rate, throughput), Resource Utilization (CPU/GPU, mem), Capacity Signals (queue depth, inflight requests), and Alerts summary.
- Visualization rules: prefer time-series for SLOs, heatmaps for per-host anomalies, and tables for top-N offenders. Avoid high-cardinality panels without a top-n filter.

Alerting standards
- Alert levels: SEV0 (platform outage), SEV1 (service degradation), SEV2 (impacting customers but partial), SEV3 (noise/informational).
- Alert content must include: symptom, probable cause(s), required impact assessment, runbook link, and suggested mitigations. Use the alert template when authoring alerts.
- Thresholds (examples):
  - api-gateway: p95 latency > 350ms for 5m (SEV1); error rate > 1.5% for 5m (SEV1); p99 latency > 800ms for 2m (SEV0 possible).
  - routing-service: 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5m (SEV1); average queue depth > 1000 (SEV1).
  - autoscaler: scale failures > 1 per 15m (SEV1); node provisioning latency > 10m (SEV2).

Alert suppression and deduplication: use alertmanager silence windows for planned maintenance and ensure alerts include fingerprint labels to allow dedupe.

5) Key runbooks (high-priority incidents)
This section lists concise, executable runbooks for the highest-importance incidents. Follow the numbered steps exactly and update the runbook if steps change. Each runbook entry contains: symptom, immediate checks, mitigation steps, rollback and postmortem actions.

5.A API Gateway: elevated 5xx rate or high p99 latency
Symptom:
- Sudden spike in 5xx errors or p99 latency across regions.
Immediate checks (5 minutes)
1) Check global grafana panel platform/api-gateway/latency-and-errors for scope (single region vs global).
2) Confirm error type: inspect logs-aggregator quick query e.g., query: "service:api-gateway 5xx | top 20 by error_message"
3) Check backend dependencies: model-serving endpoints, auth-service, and routing-service.

Mitigation steps
1) If auth-service is failing, put API gateway in degraded mode: set header routing to fallback model and enable 503-backoff.
2) If model-serving backends are overloaded, activate routing-service fallback to smaller model-variant pool by triggering rollout-manager canary policy: POST /rollouts/canary with variant=small-variant.
3) If the issue is high tail latency (KV cache thrashing), clear local caches on affected frontends and increase prefix cache hits: curl -XPOST http://node-manager/evict-cache?prefix=kvcache.

Rollforward / rollback
- Rollforward: increase capacity (scale up api-gateway replicas or route traffic to dedicated pools) and validate recovery for 20 minutes before closing the incident.
- Rollback: revert recent deploys using the rollout-manager revert API or flip traffic to previous SHA in routing rules.

Post-incident actions
1) Create a postmortem following the incident template and assign action owners.
2) Track SLO impact and customer tickets.
3) Add missing metrics or alerts discovered during the incident.

5.B Autoscaler: failure to provision nodes
Symptom:
- Autoscaler reports provisioning errors; pending pods backlog increases.
Immediate checks
1) Check autoscaler logs for error codes (quota, capacity, cloud API errors).
2) Verify cloud account quotas and region availability.
3) Inspect node-manager for repeated provisioning retries and failure reasons.

Mitigation steps
1) If quota throttling, request emergency quota increase via cloud-console contact and shift non-critical workloads to other regions.
2) If cloud API errors, temporarily scale up warm pool of pre-provisioned nodes (if available) and drain non-urgent workloads.
3) If image pull failures, verify registry credentials and revert to previous working image.

6) How-tos (dashboards, alerts, and runbook updates)
Creating or updating a dashboard
1) Clone platform template in Grafana and replace data source variables for the target service.
2) Add owner and purpose to description.
3) Add panels: SLOs, error breakdown, per-host CPU/GPU heatmap, queue depth.
4) Save with tags: platform, <service>, dashboard.
5) Create a PR in the dashboards repo (dashboards/platform) with the dashboard JSON and request review from the observability owner.

Authoring an alert rule
1) Draft alert in the prometheus rules repo (monitoring/rules/platform). Include severity label and runbook annotation.
2) Run unit tests: rules-linter --path monitoring/rules/platform.<service>.yml
3) Submit PR and request review from platform-observability.
4) After merge, create a short release note in the monitoring channel with rationale and expected noise profile.

Updating a runbook
1) Edit the canonical runbook file in the runbooks repo (runbooks/<service>.md).
2) Bump runbook version and add change log entry.
3) Notify on-call and tag the runbook owner for review.

7) Retrospective: Q3-Q4 2026 initiatives and action items
Summary of major initiatives and outcomes:
- Initiative: Autoscaler resilience improvements (led by eng-infra). Outcome: 40% reduction in scale failure incidents. Action: finish integration tests for warm pools (owner: Lena).
- Initiative: Global observability migration to managed metrics pipeline. Outcome: improved ingestion latency, but two regressions in alert fidelity. Action: add end-to-end alert testing (owner: Ben).
- Initiative: Runbook standardization. Outcome: consolidated 18 legacy runbooks into 7 canonical runbooks. Action: runbook audit every quarter (owner: Marcus).
Action items (Q1 2027 owners):
- Complete warm pool integration test harness (owner: Lena) — due 2027-01-31.
- Add end-to-end alert verification to CI (owner: Ben) — due 2027-02-15.
- Dashboard cleanup & tagging sweep (owner: Observability team) — due 2027-03-15.

8) Roadmap: Q1-Q2 2027 highlights
Q1 2027 - Finalize warm pool testing and rollout to production (reliability).
- Improve SLO coverage: add customer-impacting SLOs for dedicated deployments.
- Launch alert CI for critical alerts (reduce alert regressions).
Q2 2027 - Platform-side autoscaling policy improvements (predictive scaling pilot).
- Observability: rollout high-cardinality metric guardrails and cost-aware retention tiers.
- Developer DX: self-serve dashboard templates and one-click runbook snapshot creation.

Dependencies, milestones, and owners table:
| Milestone | Owner | Target | Dependency |
| Warm pool tests complete | eng-infra (Lena) | 2027-01-31 | internal test infra |
| Alert CI enabled | platform-observability (Ben) | 2027-02-15 | monitoring pipeline QA |
| Predictive scaling pilot | platform (Omar) | 2027-04-30 | telemetry and model signals |

9) Appendix: SLO table, escalation matrix, and example queries
SLO summary (examples)
- api-gateway: Availability 99.95% (monthly), p99 latency < 800ms (SLO target with p95 target 350ms).
- routing-service: Availability 99.9% (monthly).

Escalation matrix (short)
- On-call -> Service owner -> Platform lead -> CTO. For SEV0 incidents escalate immediately to all: #incident and start bridge.

Example Prometheus queries (for quick copy/paste)
- API gateway p99 latency (ms): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(api_request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le)) * 1000
- 5xx rate: sum(rate(api_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(api_responses_total[5m]))

Change log
- 2026-12-20: Published — consolidated dashboards and added Q1-Q2 2027 roadmap.
- 2026-11-15: Draft — initial collated content from platform team wiki and runbooks.

Feedback and maintenance
- For corrections, open a PR against this document in the docs repo or file a ticket in the platform-triage board and tag the document owner. Quarterly review cadence: platform lead will schedule a review at the start of each quarter.

End of document
